panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Ultrasound of fetus 1 showing cardiac chambers with left ventricle smaller than right ventricle and an echogenic intracardiac focus, consistent with Williams syndrome cardiac manifestations. B: Ultrasound of fetus 1 demonstrating narrowing of the ascending aorta (supravalvular aortic stenosis), a hallmark cardiovascular finding of Williams syndrome. C: Color Doppler ultrasound of fetus 1 showing tricuspid regurgitation (indicated by white arrow), a cardiac abnormality associated with Williams syndrome. D: Ultrasound of fetus 1 showing a polycystic dysplastic left kidney (indicated by white star), a renal manifestation found in this Williams syndrome fetus. E: Ultrasound of fetus 2 showing increased nuchal translucency (NT), a prenatal marker that can be associated with Williams syndrome. F: Ultrasound of fetus 2 showing an echogenic intracardiac focus (EIF), a finding noted in this Williams syndrome fetus.

panels.figure_caption: Ultrasound findings in two WS foetuses. Foetus 1 ultrasound showed (A) a left ventricle diastolic transverse diameter of 0.66cm, a right ventricle diastolic transverse diameter of 1.06cm, the left ventricle was significantly smaller than it is shown, the left ventricle was seen in the left ventricle of two echogenic solid points, the diameter about 0.13cm, 0.15cm, (B) the ascending aorta internal diameter of 0.32cm, the ascending aorta internal diameter narrowing; (C) a small amount of tricuspid regurgitation (the white arrow); (D) the left side of the polycystic dysplasia kidney (as indicated by a white star). (E) No significant cardiovascular abnormalities were seen in foetus 2; only a thickening of the NT of 2.8 mm was suggestive (double-sided arrow), and (F) an echogenic spot was seen in the left ventricle of foetus 2. Abbreviation: LA: left atrium; LV: left ventricle; RA: right atrium; RV: right ventricle; EIF: Echogenic intracardiac focus; AAO: Aorta ascendens; LK: Left kidney; NT: Nuchal translucency

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Real patient cardiac MRI from a Williams syndrome case demonstrating classic supravalvular aortic stenosis, a pathognomonic cardiovascular manifestation of the syndrome, with clear radiological findings and no excluded content. B: Real patient cardiac MRI from a Williams syndrome case showing characteristic flow pattern of supravalvular aortic stenosis at the sinotubular junction, consistent with the syndrome's typical cardiovascular presentation. C: Real patient cardiac CTA from a Williams syndrome case demonstrating classic hourglass supravalvular aortic stenosis with associated aortic membrane, a defining cardiovascular feature of the syndrome. D: Real patient cardiac CTA volume rendering from a Williams syndrome case showing both classic supravalvular aortic stenosis and associated mild supravalvular pulmonary stenosis, two characteristic cardiovascular manifestations of the syndrome.
panels.attribution_text: Micari et al. Advanced Multimodality Cardiovascular Imaging of Supravalvular Aortic Stenosis in Williams-Beuren Syndrome.. Circulation. Cardiovascular imaging 2024. doi:10.1161/circimaging.124.016733. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure Figure.
panels.figure_caption: Multimodality imaging assessment of supravalvular aortic stenosis in a 37-year-old man. A, Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) balanced steady-state free-precession sequence along the left ventricular outflow tract, showing turbulent blood flow above the aortic valve during systole (red arrow). B, Cardiac MRI through-plane phase-contrast velocity mapping obtained at the sinotubular junction level shows a crescent-like appearance of the aortic flow (red arrowhead). in_text_mentions: A 15 year old boy presented in a clinic with symptoms of dyspnea (NYHA, Class I). He was short (height less than 3rd centile) with global developmental delay, a very sociable personality, and a hoarse voice. A physical examination showed dysmorphic facial features like periorbital fullness, full cheeks with prominent naso-labial folds, thick lips, and widely spaced permanent dentition. Clinically, Williams syndrome was suspected [Figure 1].
